content.coreClaim: Neoliberalism is not only a policy program but a rationality: a way of thinking and feeling in which competition is the universal metric of human worth and every individual is a small enterprise. It did not just change markets; it changed what people expect of themselves.
content.mechanism: Harvey's A Brief History of Neoliberalism (2005) tells the institutional story — the think tanks, the crises, the class restoration — while Dardot and Laval's The New Way of the World (2009) supplies the deeper claim. Neoliberalism, on their account, is a rationality in Foucault's sense: a coherent logic that reorganizes not only the state and the economy but subjectivity itself. Its core is the generalization of the enterprise form: the individual becomes human capital, an entrepreneur of the self, perpetually investing in skills, branding, and networks, perpetually competing. What distinguishes this from older liberalisms is that competition stops being a market mechanism and becomes an existential imperative — one that applies equally to the unemployed worker, the university, the parent, and the state itself. Failure, within this rationality, is not structural; it is personal. The person who did not upskill, pivot, or brand themselves adequately did not lose; they failed to compete.
content.canonicalExample: The collapse of WeWork in September 2019 is the rationality's most literal corporate form. The company sold not office space but community and mission — 'elevate the world's consciousness' — and its charismatic founder's valuation rhetoric lifted it toward $47 billion before its IPO documents revealed the underlying economics. What the episode exposed was the logic operating in pure form: a company whose product was the image of enterprise itself, valued on narrative and growth metrics, staffed by workers hired for their 'energy', in an economy where even community had become a value proposition. The IPO's failure did not discredit the rationality; the founder's subsequent relaunches showed it absorbing the failure, converting even bankruptcy into further evidence of entrepreneurial resilience.
content.conceptualTension: The framework is contested at its edges rather than its core. Some critics argue 'neoliberalism' has become a catch-all that explains everything and therefore nothing, and that the contemporary conjuncture — platform economies, techno-feudalism (6.7), surveillance capitalism (6.8) — has mutated beyond the 1970s–2000s formation the concept was built to describe. The disciplined use treats it as the dominant rationality of the late twentieth century, still operating but now hybridized with newer logics — and names which mechanism is doing the work in any given case rather than reaching for the label alone.
content.connectionNode: Neoliberal rationality is the subjectivity-side of 3.6 (Cultural Hegemony): it is the common sense that hegemony installed, experienced as individual aspiration. It also inherits from 4.2 (Disciplinary Society) — the enterprise-self is the norm internalized — and it supplies the demand-side pressure behind 6.2 (Accumulation by Dispossession), whose enclosures this rationality makes feel like opportunities.
content.microPraxis: Notice, today, where you treated yourself as a project to optimize — sleep, output, image, network. Separate the project from the person running it. The entrepreneur-of-self is a governance, not a nature, and noticing the governance is the first distance from it.
content.zeigarnikHook: You have been trained to experience yourself as human capital. What would remain of you if you stopped accounting for yourself entirely? And what does the fear of that question tell you about who installed it?

content.coreClaim: The enclosure of common resources is not a historical prelude to capitalism; it is a continuous present. Land, water, knowledge, genetic material, and attention are being fenced and priced today, and the fences are called modernization.
content.mechanism: Harvey's The New Imperialism (2003) coined the term to update Marx's 'primitive accumulation' — the violence Marx described as capitalism's founding act, when commoners were separated from land, tools, and the means of subsistence. Harvey's argument is that the process never stopped: whenever ordinary accumulation stalls, capital falls back on dispossession — privatizing public assets, commodifying commons, expropriating knowledge, turning public goods into rent-bearing property. The mechanism matters because it explains the resilience of capital through crisis: the pool of things not yet commodified is the system's reserve tank. Water systems, seeds, genomes, public space, personal data — each wave of enclosure presents itself as efficiency, and each is the same move: something people held in common becomes something someone owns.
content.canonicalExample: The Cochabamba water war of 2000 is the modern archetype. Bolivia, under pressure from lenders, privatized the water system of its third-largest city through a concession to a consortium led by Bechtel; the contract extended even to rainwater harvesting, and rates for some households reportedly rose to a third of their income. In April 2000, after months of escalating protests, the government cancelled the concession and returned the system to public control — the first major reversal of a water privatization of its era. The episode matters beyond its outcome: it made the enclosure visible as enclosure. What had been a commons — rain, wells, customary systems — had been, briefly and legally, property, and the population's revolt was the recognition that something which had never been theirs alone had been taken.
content.conceptualTension: The debates here are about boundaries. Critics ask what, in a complex economy, genuinely counts as dispossession versus ordinary market exchange — if every purchase is the pricing of something, the concept risks losing its edge. Harvey's reply is that the distinction is real but historical: dispossession names the moments when the commodity form is imposed on things that previously existed outside it, and the test is the one Cochabamba poses — did the change require force, law, or debt to make it stick?
content.connectionNode: Accumulation by dispossession is the economic mechanism beneath 3.3 (Social Reproduction Theory): the unpaid care economy is a commons capital has partially enclosed through wage labor's dependence on it. The same enclosure exhausts the soil, water, and energy commons of 6.4 (Metabolic Rift), and the dispossessed, as 4.5 (Racial Capitalism) shows, have always been sorted by race.
content.microPraxis: List three things that used to be common in your own lifetime and are now charged for — water refills, a seat, a moment of attention, access to knowledge. For each, name the enclosure: the rule, the price, the wall. The price appeared where the commons was taken, and the list is longer than you expect.
content.zeigarnikHook: The reserve of unenclosed things is what keeps capital alive through crisis. What will be the last commons to go — and what will it be like to live on the other side of its fence?

content.coreClaim: The market economy rests on care that the market does not pay for — children raised, bodies maintained, elders tended, grief absorbed — and the arrangement is gendered and globalized. The care economy is not a sector; it is the foundation.
content.mechanism: Where 3.3 established the unpaid foundation, this lesson follows the money's attempt to price it. Federici's framework: reproductive labor produces the worker, and its unwaged status is what keeps the wage affordable — the wage is a subsidy from the unwaged. Folbre's economics formalizes the point: the care sector, where it is waged, is systematically undervalued precisely because it is associated with the unpaid work of women; its work is relational, resistant to productivity metrics, and therefore invisible to the accounting that sets pay. The Global South enters as the care chain: migrant women leave their own families to care for others' children and elders in the Global North, exporting care from poorer to richer households in a global transfer of reproductive labor. The system's stability depends on the chain continuing, and the chain's links are wearing.
content.canonicalExample: The French pension reform strikes of 2023 put the care economy's arithmetic on the streets. The government's plan to raise the retirement age from 62 to 64 provoked the largest sustained demonstrations in France in decades, from January through June — and the opposition's core argument was about the accounting of a life's work: the reform, its critics argued, fell hardest on those whose labor was already uncounted and unpaid, women above all, whose careers are interrupted by care and whose pensions are lower for it. What the conflict made explicit was the hidden ledger this lesson describes: the difference between retirement at 62 and 64 is a claim about which years of a person's life count as work, and the unpaid years of care have never counted. The strikes did not stop the law; they made the subsidy visible, which is what the analysis of the care economy exists to do.
content.conceptualTension: The contested question is strategic, and it replays the 3.3 debate at the level of policy. Does pricing care — wages for care work, credits for caregivers — begin to correct the subsidy, or does it legitimize the gendered allocation of the work itself? The positions range from waging care as a stopgap to reconfiguring the working day entirely, and the debate over the French reform shows each position carrying real political consequences.
content.connectionNode: This lesson is the policy-level completion of 3.3 (Social Reproduction Theory), and its global care chain is the reproductive form of 4.6 (Coloniality of Power) — care flows along the colonial matrix's channels. And the debt is collected, in 6.9 (The Precariat), as time poverty — the care economy's bill, presented to the individual.
content.microPraxis: List the care labor — yours and others' — that your day depended on, and total its hours. Then ask which of those hours were priced, and by whom. The productivity of your day rested on an unpriced foundation, and the exercise is to see the foundation as foundation.
content.zeigarnikHook: The economy's productivity is subsidized by unpaid care. What would happen to every price you know if the subsidy were withdrawn? And what does your reluctance to imagine it reveal about who the subsidy serves?

content.coreClaim: Capitalism breaks the material cycles between society and nature. The nutrients taken from the soil, the carbon taken from the ground, do not return — and the break is not an accident of industrialism but a structural feature of an economy organized around extraction.
content.mechanism: Marx's concept, reconstructed by John Bellamy Foster, comes from Marx's reading of the agricultural chemist Justus von Liebig. In pre-industrial agriculture, the nutrients removed by harvest return to the soil through the waste of those who eat it. Capitalist agriculture breaks the loop: food travels from country to city, and the nutrients in the city's waste are dumped into rivers and seas rather than returned to the fields. The rift — Marx's word — is the rupture of the metabolic cycle, and it has a second instance in energy: fossil carbon, sequestered over geological time, is burned into the atmosphere in centuries, with no cycle that returns it. Foster's argument is that Marx, far from being a Promethean cheerleader of industry, was among the first analysts of ecological crisis — and that the rift is structural: an economy that must grow through extraction cannot close the loops it breaks.
content.canonicalExample: The guano trade of the nineteenth century is the rift's first global crisis, and it is strangely instructive. When European soils depleted, the fertilizer that sustained them came from Peruvian guano islands — centuries of accumulated bird excrement mined out and shipped across the Atlantic. The trade peaked in the 1850s; the Chincha Islands were worked nearly bare; Spain and Peru fought a war over the residue in the 1860s. The episode's modern echo runs through the Gulf of Mexico, where nitrogen fertilizer running off Midwestern farms feeds an oxygen-depleted dead zone that NOAA has measured annually since 1985 — in 2023, around three thousand square miles of water unable to sustain marine life. The guano is gone and replaced by synthetic nitrogen; the rift is the same: nutrients extracted in one place, concentrated in another, cycling nowhere.
content.conceptualTension: The contested question is whether the rift can be closed within capitalism. Ecological modernizers argue that circular economies, regenerative agriculture, and decarbonization can re-close the loops without abandoning the system — that the rift was a technical choice, not a structural necessity. Foster's school replies that the profit motive structurally resists closure, since returning nutrients and carbon costs more than extracting new ones, and the history of every prior 'efficiency' — guano, synthetic fertilizer, fracking — has been a new rift opened to patch the old. The argument is the ecological fault line of the present.
content.connectionNode: The metabolic rift is the material history beneath 5.5 (Planetary Boundaries): the boundaries are the rift's planetary measurement. The commons being enclosed here is the nutrient cycle itself, which ties the lesson to 6.2 (Accumulation by Dispossession) and grounds the ecological vector that 1.9 (Two-Eyed Seeing) names relationally.
content.microPraxis: Trace one material you depend on — water, food, a metal — from extraction to disposal in your own day, and locate the place where the cycle breaks. Stay on the single break; leave the whole chain alone. The rift is not abstract; it is a specific break in a specific cycle you personally depend on.
content.zeigarnikHook: The system's survival has always depended on finding new rifts to patch the old ones. What happens when the last reserves are opened — and is 'sustainability' a repair of the cycle or a name for its slowest possible exhaustion?

content.coreClaim: Economic models do not simply describe markets; they remake them. A theory, once enough people act on it, changes the reality it was built to mirror.
content.mechanism: The performativity thesis, developed by Callon and by MacKenzie's An Engine, Not a Camera (2006), borrows Austin's word from 3.2: an economic model can be a performative utterance. The strongest case is Black-Scholes: the options pricing formula of 1973 did not merely measure the derivatives market; traders began pricing options with the formula, so the market converged toward the model's assumptions, and the model became, in part, the engine of the thing it described. MacKenzie's ethnographic research at the Chicago exchanges documented the loop in detail: the formula's assumptions about volatility were literally built into trading practice, terminals, and hedges. The thesis's power is that it inverts the economist's self-image: economics is not the science that observes the economy from outside; it is a participant that alters its object, and the alteration is strongest precisely where the theory is most widely believed.
content.canonicalExample: Black Monday, October 19, 1987, is the thesis's dramatic test. In the years before the crash, institutional investors had adopted 'portfolio insurance' — a hedging strategy derived from the options-pricing framework, which called for selling more and more as prices fell, in order to replicate a put option synthetically. On Black Monday, when prices began to fall, the insurers sold; the selling pushed prices lower, which triggered more selling, and the Dow fell 22.6 percent in a single day — still its largest one-day percentage drop. The model had assumed continuous markets and liquid trading; in practice, the strategy's own execution changed the market it was operating in. The mechanism the crash exposed was performative in the strict sense: the theory had generated the behavior that broke the theory.
content.conceptualTension: The thesis's critics — among them orthodox economists and some sociologists — argue that 'performativity' blurs together things of very different strengths: from loose influence (theories shaping attention) to strong construction (theories making reality), and only the weak claims are clearly supported. The disputed territory is the strong version: does the economy have any behavior independent of the models applied to it? The thesis's best answer is Black Monday's: the independence exists, but it is shaped — sometimes violently — by the very act of modeling it.
content.connectionNode: Performativity is the economic instance of 5.9 (Reflexivity): the observer's loop, run through trading floors. The word descends from Austin's speech acts, as does 3.2 (Performativity in Butler's sense), and the lesson extends 1.4 (Map ≠ Territory): here the maps stop describing and start building the terrain.
content.microPraxis: Notice one metric you optimize against — a price, a ranking, a score, a share count. For two minutes, ask how your optimizing is making the metric more real, and whether the metric tracks anything outside the optimization. The model is partly making the market it claims to measure, and you are one of its instruments.
content.zeigarnikHook: Enough people believed an economic model, and it became true. Which models are currently making your economy true, who chose them, and what happens when belief in one of them fails?

content.coreClaim: Platforms are infrastructure for extraction. They do not mainly produce goods or services; they position themselves between other people's exchanges and collect rent on every one of them, in data and in fees.
content.mechanism: Srnicek's Platform Capitalism (2016) analyzes the platform as a business model before it is a technology. A platform is digital infrastructure that intermediates between users; its strategic position — the choke point — lets it extract from both sides of every interaction it hosts. The taxonomy helps: advertising platforms mine attention and behavioral data; cloud platforms rent computing power; industrial platforms orchestrate manufacturing; product platforms convert other firms' goods into rent (the app store, the marketplace); lean platforms own no assets and no workers — Uber owns no cars, Airbnb no rooms — but collect the toll on every ride and stay. The data point is load-bearing for the whole category: platforms are not neutral pipes; they are recorders, and the record of every interaction becomes the input to prediction and pricing, so the platform's advantage compounds with every transaction it hosts. This is why platforms tend toward monopoly — the choke point's logic, not market failure, produces concentration.
content.canonicalExample: California's Proposition 22, passed in November 2020, is the platform model's political milestone. The ballot measure, backed by Uber, Lyft, and DoorDash at a cost of over $200 million — the most expensive ballot campaign in California history — exempted app-based drivers from the state's new law that would have classified them as employees. The campaign is instructive in itself: the platforms argued that flexibility was what drivers wanted, and the measure passed, establishing gig drivers as a legally distinct category with some benefits and no employment relationship. What the episode made visible is the platform's structural position: the companies could afford the largest ballot campaign in state history precisely because the classification question determined the size of their rent — and the outcome locked in a labor category that the platforms themselves had written.
content.conceptualTension: The main debate is whether the platform is a new mode of production or an old one with better logistics. Critics of the novelty claim point out that tolls on infrastructure, monopsony over labor, and data-driven pricing all have nineteenth-century precedents. Srnicek's own account is careful on this: the platform is a mutation of capitalism, not its successor — a position that the techno-feudalism thesis of 6.7 contests from the other direction, arguing the mutation has become a new regime.
content.connectionNode: Platform capitalism is the present form of 6.2 (Accumulation by Dispossession): the choke point is the new enclosure. Downstream, 6.8 (Surveillance Capitalism) is what advertising platforms do with the data, and 7.5 (Network Effects) is the mechanism that makes the choke point stick.
content.microPraxis: List the platforms you cannot exit — the ones where 'leaving' means leaving the field: the marketplace, the app store, the workplace's platform. For each, name the rent it extracts and the lock-in that enforces it. The 'choice' of platform is largely the choice of which landlord, and the list is the map of your tenancies.
content.zeigarnikHook: The economy's choke points are owned, and the rest of us are tenants. What would it take to build infrastructure nobody rents out? And what does the history of previous commons tell you about what happens to it?

content.coreClaim: The market is being displaced by digital fiefdoms. What the dominant platforms extract is no longer primarily profit from exchange but rent from the infrastructure itself — a toll on every transaction that passes through their territory.
content.mechanism: Varoufakis's Techno-Feudalism (2023) argues that the platform economy has changed the mode of extraction. In capitalism proper, profit comes from production and exchange; in the new order, the dominant platforms extract 'cloud rent' — payments that users, merchants, and even cloudless firms must make for access to the digital territory where exchange now happens. The feudal analogy is precise on one point: the serf did not sell his labor to the lord; he owed the lord for the right to work the land. The platform's users and merchants owe for the right to transact, to reach customers, to exist as a business online. Varoufakis's supporting claims: the platforms' capital now finances itself increasingly through its own issued instruments; the price mechanism has been replaced inside the platforms by algorithmic direction; and the central banks have become, in his phrase, the platforms' fiefs' financiers. The thesis's ambition is to name a regime change, not a business model.
content.canonicalExample: Epic Games v. Apple, tried in 2021, is the rent relation litigated in public. Epic sought to sell digital items inside its game on iPhones without paying Apple's 30 percent commission on every transaction; Apple removed Fortnite from the App Store; the trial, and the September 2021 ruling, produced a split decision — Apple largely won the commission on in-app purchases, while being required to permit alternative payment links. What the case displayed, whatever the verdicts, is the structure: a toll on transactions that occur within territory owned by a platform, paid not for a service rendered but for permission to operate. Whether one calls it a commission, a tax, or rent, the relation is the one Varoufakis names — and the fact that the litigation concerned the toll's size, not its legitimacy, is itself part of the thesis.
content.conceptualTension: This lesson's status is actively-debated, and the critical note must be honored. The strongest objection is that cloud rent is still profit — platform revenue ultimately comes from selling goods, services, and advertising to consumers, however mediated — so the feudal analogy overstates the break with capitalism. Critics in Jacobin (2023) and the Network Cultures review (2024) have pressed versions of this argument, and Srnicek's platform-capitalism framing of 6.6 contests the same ground from the inside. The thesis's defenders reply that the structural position — ownership of the territory on which others' capitalism runs — is the point, whatever the accounting label. The honest posture is to hold both framings and ask of each new episode: rent or profit, and does the distinction change the politics?
content.connectionNode: Techno-feudalism is the regime-change reading of 6.6 (Platform Capitalism) — same platforms, different name for what they extract. It connects to 6.2 (Accumulation by Dispossession), whose enclosures here reach their logical form, and to 7.5 (Network Effects), the topology that makes fiefdoms defensible.
content.microPraxis: On your phone, list the platforms whose infrastructure you could not avoid today — the store, the cloud, the marketplace, the search engine. For each, name the rent it extracted from you, in money, data, or attention. The 'market' you think you operate in is their fiefdom, and the exercise is to feel the tolls.
content.zeigarnikHook: The market you inhabit is partly a fiefdom and partly a market. How would you know which you are in at any moment — and who profits from your not knowing?

content.coreClaim: Human behavioral data has become a raw material extracted at scale, processed into prediction products, and sold to those who would modify future behavior. The user is not the customer; the user's behavior is the product.
content.mechanism: Zuboff's The Age of Surveillance Capitalism (2019) describes the model with a forensic vocabulary. Behavioral surplus: the data generated by users beyond what any service strictly needs — the trail of searches, pauses, locations, and hesitations that no one asked for and that keeps accumulating. The surplus is rendered into prediction products: profiles of what individuals will do, feel, or buy, sold to advertisers and other actors who want behavior modified in advance. Zuboff's sharpest claims are about novelty — this is not the same as industrial capitalism's surveillance of workers, because the extraction is unilateral, the surplus belongs to the company, and the target of the machinery is not labor but behavior itself — and about power: the companies' knowledge asymmetry becomes an instrumentality, in her word, that shapes what users can think to want. The term's influence and its contestation both stem from how much weight is placed on that novelty claim.
content.canonicalExample: The Cambridge Analytica scandal of March 2018 is the model's public proof. A researcher collected data from millions of Facebook users — not only those who took a personality quiz but their friends, through the platform's data-sharing rules at the time — and the data passed to a political consultancy that used psychographic profiles to target political advertising in the 2016 US election and the Brexit campaign. The scandal's revelations — 87 million affected profiles, congressional hearings, a $5 billion FTC fine for Facebook — displayed every element of the model at once: behavioral surplus harvested without meaningful consent, rendered into prediction products, and deployed to modify behavior at scale. What the episode did not change is worth noting: the underlying business model remained, because the model was not the scandal; the scandal was the model made visible.
content.conceptualTension: The framing is contested, and the critical note names the objection: some political economists argue Zuboff overstates novelty — capitalism has always accumulated information about workers and consumers, and advertising has always aimed at behavior — so 'surveillance capitalism' is a new name for an old logic, not a new logic. Zuboff's defense is that the unilateral extraction of behavioral surplus, at the speed and scale of machine learning, changes the power relation qualitatively: the difference between a shopkeeper's intuition and a prediction product is the difference between a telescope and a panopticon. The debate is live, and the lesson's honest position is that both sides are partly right.
content.connectionNode: Surveillance capitalism is what advertising platforms do with the data 6.6 (Platform Capitalism) collects at the choke point. The connection to 4.2 (Disciplinary Society) is direct: the panopticon here is privatized and predictive. And in 7.4 (Algorithmic Governance), the prediction products leave the marketplace and enter bail, credit, and welfare decisions.
content.microPraxis: List the behavioral data you generated before lunch today — searches, scrolls, stops, purchases, locations. Name who likely captured each piece and what prediction it feeds. The self-as-resource is not a metaphor; the mining is continuous, and the exercise is to catch it running.
content.zeigarnikHook: Your behavior is mined to predict and shape what you will want next. What is the difference between your desire and its prediction? And at what point does the prediction become the desire?

content.coreClaim: A growing class of workers is defined by what it lacks: stable employment, secure income, predictable time, and political voice. Precarity is not the exception to the contemporary labor regime; it is the regime.
content.mechanism: Standing's The Precariat (2011) proposes that precarity is not just a condition of particular jobs but the basis of an emerging class, defined negatively — by the absence of the securities that organized labor once delivered: labor security, employment security, income security, and representation. The class is heterogeneous — the gig worker, the adjunct lecturer, the platform freelancer, the temp — but shares a position: work is episodic, risk is individual, and the future is perpetually uncertain. Fraser's contribution is the analytic frame: precarity is produced, not fallen into — the state and capital offload risk onto workers while retaining control of the conditions that create it. The time dimension is the sharpest symptom: the precarious worker is time-poor, because survival requires constant availability, constant searching, constant readiness — the work of maintaining the possibility of work, which no wage pays for and which eats the hours that used to build anything else.
content.canonicalExample: The 2023 Hollywood strikes — the Writers Guild from May, joined by SAG-AFTRA actors in July, lasting into November — were the precariat's highest-profile revolt. The writers' core demands were the precarity's core grievances: streaming had turned television writing from a career into a gig — shorter seasons, smaller rooms, no residuals — and the studios' plans for AI threatened to automate the remaining entry-level work, cutting the ladder entirely. What the double strike made public was the structure beneath the glamour: the most visible cultural industry in the world now runs largely on insecure, episodic labor, with the risk borne by workers who cannot predict their own next quarter. The settlements, with their AI protections and residual formulas, were partial wins inside the regime — and the regime remained.
content.conceptualTension: Whether the precariat is a class at all is the contested question. Labor sociologists object that its members occupy contradictory positions — the adjunct and the delivery driver share insecurity but not interests — and that the category can fragment class analysis rather than consolidate it. Standing's reply is that classes in formation always begin as negative coalitions, defined by shared dispossession before shared identity. The debate matters because it decides whether 'the precariat' can act politically as one subject, or whether precarity names only a shared condition.
content.connectionNode: The precariat is the labor-market form of 6.1 (Neoliberal Rationality): the enterprise-self's structural condition. The tie to 6.3 (Care Economy) is arithmetic: time poverty there is partly unpaid care's debt collected at the individual level. And 7.7 (Liquid Modernity) supplies the habitat — dissolved institutions — in which the precariat lives.
content.microPraxis: Estimate the time you spent this week just sustaining the conditions of work — commuting, scheduling, billing, applying, staying available — versus actually working. Write the ratio down. Then ask what the ratio does to your capacity for anything else: organizing, learning, resting, refusing. The time-poverty is not personal; it is structural, and the structure is legible in the ratio.
content.zeigarnikHook: The system that makes you time-poor also blames you for not using your time well. What would it take to hear 'you're not managing your time' as a statement about the economy rather than about you?

content.coreClaim: The economy should operate between a social foundation — beneath which human needs go unmet — and an ecological ceiling — above which planetary systems break. Growth is not the goal; the space between the two rings is.
content.mechanism: Raworth's Doughnut Economics (2017) redraws the economy as a target rather than a rocket. The inner ring is the social foundation: the minimum thresholds for health, education, housing, income, voice, and dignity, drawn from the Sustainable Development Goals. The outer ring is the ecological ceiling: the planetary boundaries of 5.5. Between the rings lies the doughnut — the safe and just space in which humanity's task is not to grow but to meet every person's foundation without breaching any planetary limit. The framework's target of critique is the twentieth century's dominant image: GDP growth as the measure of success, decoupled from both distribution and ecology. Raworth's argument is that the image is not only inadequate but dangerous — growth now concentrates at the top and consumes the ceiling — and that the alternative is regenerative and distributive by design, rather than redistributive after the fact. The doughnut's power is diagrammatic: it lets a city council see at a glance whether its policies are expanding the doughnut or pinching it.
content.canonicalExample: Amsterdam is the framework's flagship experiment. In April 2020 the city formally adopted the doughnut as its official policy framework, and the subsequent years produced its first concrete applications: post-pandemic recovery plans assessed against the social foundation, housing policy that capped new construction for low- and middle-income residents, and — most emblematic — the decision to halve the use of primary raw materials by 2030, evaluated explicitly against the outer ring. The experiment is young, its results contested, and its ambition is the point: the first time a major city has attempted to run its economy against two absolute boundaries instead of one open-ended growth curve. Whether Amsterdam's doughnut proves reproducible or a well-publicized exception is one of the live empirical questions of ecological economics.
content.conceptualTension: The critical note is precise: the doughnut is a normative framework, not a settled economic model. Ecological economists debate the foundations — are the SDG thresholds the right ones, and can a single planetary ceiling be distributed fairly between rich and poor regions? Growth economists object that the framework under-specifies the transition: between the rings, where does investment come from, and what pays for the social foundation without growth's surpluses? Raworth's answer — that the questions are design problems, and that growth has become the wrong measure even where it is not yet the wrong outcome — keeps the debate where it belongs: on the trade-offs, not the slogan.
content.connectionNode: The doughnut operationalizes 5.5 (Planetary Boundaries) as an economic floor-and-ceiling pair, and it answers 6.4 (Metabolic Rift) with a design brief — the regenerative economy is the rift's closure attempted. It also inherits the critique of 6.1 (Neoliberal Rationality): growth as identity is the rationality's metric, and the doughnut is its replacement diagram.
content.microPraxis: Draw the doughnut with yourself in it: on one axis, are your own needs being met; on the other, is your footprint within the ceiling? Locate yourself, then ask what would have to change — for you, for your city, for your industry — to move toward the space between the rings without assuming growth will get you there. The map is personal before it is political, and it is drawn with two lines.
content.zeigarnikHook: The economy you were promised keeps growing toward a ceiling it cannot see. What would 'enough' feel like — and is the harder problem the ceiling, or the fact that no one in your life can describe what enough would mean?
